יכול אפילו לראות אותך בוכה, / לא יכול להרשות לעצמי ביי אחרון. / עם החברות שלך, לא פחדתן, לביאות עד שאתן מתות". משפחתה מתכננת הקמת עמותה, "המספרים של אושר", שבמסגרתה סטודנטים יעבירו שיעורי תגבור במתמטיקה בתמורה למלגת לימודים.
cvEn: Osher Simha Barzilai, daughter of Tiki and Lior, was born on 21 Sivan 5764 (10 June 2004) in the local council of Mazkeret Batya. She was the sister of Sapir, Eden, Yarin and Yarden, who were older than her, and of Hen, who was younger. Osher (Simha) grew up and was educated in Mazkeret Batya. From the day she was born, she brought Osher, meaning happiness, and Simha, meaning joy, to her family, as her names said. As a baby, her older siblings competed over who would look after her, who would feed her and who would hold her. As a child she was beautiful, smiling, talented and independent. Her warm personality lit up every room she entered, and she was always surrounded by friends who were drawn to her optimism, the warmth she radiated and the sensitivity that characterized her. She was endlessly generous to others and loved people. She stood out for her high intelligence, which showed in how quickly she grasped new material, how deeply she explored subjects that interested her, and her strong ability to learn on her own. For example, she taught herself to play the piano and the guitar by watching lessons on YouTube. She was a student at the Rabin High School in Mazkeret Batya, in the biology track. She excelled in her studies and was drawn mainly to the sciences. Out of her generous heart, and her wish to help and advance others, she volunteered to tutor students who struggled with mathematics. At the same time, she joined the national neuroscience class of the Davidson Institute of Science Education, the educational arm of the Weizmann Institute of Science, and studied there toward her matriculation exams in five units. She enjoyed the studies in the track, said she wanted to study medicine in the future, and dreamed of becoming a brain surgeon. Her drive for excellence, her outstanding achievements and her desire to help and heal showed that she was on the right path to making the dream come true. The track coordinator said: "Even within this special group of gifted students, Osher stood out as one of the most impressive students. She captivated us not only with her curiosity, intelligence and original thinking, but above all with the empathy and kindness she showed toward everyone around her, students and teachers alike." Osher was responsible and efficient, and knew how to balance her studies with social life, volunteering, outings and pleasures. For four years she volunteered devotedly with Magen David Adom (MDA), missed no shift and trained young volunteers. She loved to travel in Israel and abroad, and tried challenging activities such as rappelling, skydiving, water skiing and horseback riding. She was well-groomed, radiant and "always smiling," as she described herself on Instagram. She made the most of every moment in life, and liked to say: "The question is not how much time you have, but how you divide the time you have." At school she met Ori, and they became a loving couple. "Osher was the best partner I could have asked for," he said. "We grew up and matured together. She helped me shape my character and become a better person. Four years of being together made those four years the best of my life. We always talked about the future we would share, about marriage and children and where we would live. She was the best thing that ever happened to me." When she finished high school, she expressed a wish to serve in the IDF in an interesting and meaningful role. On 1 January 2023 she enlisted in the IDF. She was accepted to the operations sergeants course (Samabatzit) and graduated as the top student of the course and of her company. She was assigned as an operations sergeant in the Hagefen Brigade, the northern brigade of the Gaza Division. She served at the Nahal Oz outpost near the border with the Gaza Strip. Alongside her served dozens of observers and forces from the Golani Brigade and the 7th Armored Brigade, whose mission was to defend the Nahal Oz sector and the outpost within it. Osher loved the role and her fellow soldiers. They said she was a professional operations sergeant with leadership ability, who brought much light and joy to the operations room, and who always acted with modesty and sensitivity. She knew the sector inside out, and although she reported tension and heightened activity beyond the border fence, she felt protected and safe at the outpost. She planned to go to officers' course in February 2024. The distance imposed on her from her partner during her service did not harm the deep bond between them. She wrote to him longingly: "To my best friend, my pillar, the person who understands me most in the world. I wish I could hear from you more. The uncertainty about when I will next see you is killing me. My time with you is short, but the most meaningful in the world to me. I miss you more than anything in life, and already want to hug you and wrap you up without ever letting go." On the eve of Sukkot 5784, Osher and Ori went on short leave from their units, and after dinner they celebrated at a party. It was the last time they met. On Saturday, 22 Tishrei, Simchat Torah 5784, 7 October 2023, at six thirty in the morning, the Hamas terror organization launched a surprise attack on Israel. Under cover of massive rocket and missile fire from the Gaza Strip into wide areas of the country, thousands of terrorists infiltrated by land, sea and air, and began a murderous assault on the communities of the Gaza envelope, on Sderot, Ofakim and Netivot, at the Supernova music festival near Re'im and Nir Oz, on IDF bases and on travelers on the roads in the area. The terrorists murdered some eight hundred civilians in their homes and in their cars, after committing grave crimes against them. They abducted hundreds of Israelis to the Gaza Strip, and destroyed, looted and set fire to homes and property. Hundreds of soldiers, police officers, security personnel and members of local emergency squads fell in battle. That morning, a war began. On that Saturday Osher was on shift in the operations room at the Nahal Oz outpost. At six thirty in the morning the observers spotted terrorists near the border fence, and within minutes more than a hundred terrorists stormed the outpost. Fifty more terrorists later joined them. Osher immediately understood that this was an unusual event, and took command. She directed the Golani soldiers fighting in the base itself, and guided forces to the nearby communities and the outposts under attack, and in this way saved the lives of many people. During the battle she managed to write to her partner: "I love you. Tell everyone I'm okay for now. I'm in the operations room." At 10:23 she wrote to her family: "Pray for me." When she was offered a chance to escape the operations room, she refused to abandon it and leave her fellow soldiers behind. Osher was the only operations sergeant in the room, and carried out her role resourcefully and responsibly while alone at her post for about twenty-five minutes. During that time she also prepared the personnel roster for the officers who asked for it, and let the women in the room speak to their families on her phone. The battle review determined that she performed exemplarily until the last moment. For seven days she was listed as missing. On Saturday, 14 October 2023, the family received the news of her death. On that day several dozen soldiers fell at the Nahal Oz outpost. Corporal Osher Simha Barzilai fell in battle on 22 Tishrei 5784 (7 October 2023). After her death she was posthumously promoted to Sergeant. She was nineteen and a half years old when she fell. She was laid to rest in the military section of the cemetery in Mazkeret Batya. She left behind her parents and five brothers and sisters. Her mother eulogized her: "The pain is immense. We have suffered the worst of all, and I know nothing will ever be the same. But I am not going to be a bereaved mother. I am going to be a mother who can. Who can once again unite, gather the family, strengthen, lift up, grieve together, and from here grow, become stronger, commemorate, and even expand. I am a proud mother, with my head held high. Proud of the daughter who, in her death, left us life. We will continue her legacy, her drive for excellence, with joy of life, social life, trips and endless pleasures. Many have spoken about her, and I could go on for hours. I know my private heroine better than anyone, and she has now become everyone's heroine." Her sister Yarden eulogized her: "Osher, your smile was spread everywhere you walked. You left behind parents and siblings in pain, an endless list of friends, and a partner who accompanied you for four years. Osher, my dear, for all of us, forever, there will be a hole in the heart in your shape." Her sister Hen eulogized her: "I don't know who I should be angry at now, or whether I am even allowed to be angry. Every night I ask God, why did this happen? Why did He take my sister to Him? Mom said it's because she was a hero. Osher could have escaped, but chose to stay and help her soldiers. Dad said God takes the best. I told Dad I don't understand why God doesn't leave the good people and take the bad ones to Him. "Everyone shared my grief at the funeral. When the rabbi finished, Mom whispered in my ear that now I had to cry, but I had no tears. I saw a white butterfly and smiled to myself. My brother said to me, 'What are you doing? You have to cry now.' I quickly dropped the smile and made a sad face. I looked at the grave and thought about my friend and our fight. I remembered how much I had cried then, but the tears did not come now. "After the shiva, when everyone had returned to their homes, I went to my room, put my head on my pillow and Osher's, and thought about Osher in the operations room with her soldiers, about Osher who volunteered with MDA, about Osher who took care of her soldiers when the terrorists struck them, about Osher who was an excellent student, about Osher who left me alone. I asked her why, and only then did the tears come." Tamar wrote: "Osher, my beloved, the best friend in the world, the one who gives everything for those around her, no matter when. How I loved being with you, laughing with you, talking with you for hours. I will never forget that you always helped me with everything and solved every problem for me, because you always knew what to do. Your smile does not leave my mind, and I cannot grasp that I will not see you again. Everyone who knew you knows how pure you were, with a heart of gold, and how smart and outstanding you were in everything you did in your life. You were an inspiration to me. Osher, my heart is broken that you were killed there like that, our heroine. Even in your last hours you did everything to help everyone, because that is how you always were." Keren, a student at the Davidson Institute, wrote: "Osher, you taught me to make coffee, to study only in bed, to stop being late everywhere, to sit and study even when I had no energy. And above all, you brought a lot of Osher and joy into my life."
